clue.text: University clubs keeping old vessels

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for university
bats are clubs used to hit a ball
O is the usual abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Student rowing clubs hang on to their ancient boats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' suggests societies, which fits University; here it means sports bats. U-boat is the German term for a submarine.
explanation.definitionFit: U-boats were German submarines, a kind of naval vessel.

clue.text: Blessed? He's a very naughty boy!

blocks.note: first meaning: the forename of the booming actor ... Blessed
second meaning: the line from Monty Python's Life of ..., where his mother says he is not the Messiah

explanation.walkthrough: 'Blessed' looks like a religious adjective, which suits the Messiah joke, but it is the surname of the actor Brian Blessed.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves point to a person called Brian: an actor's first name and the Monty Python film character.

clue.text: Principal investor offering chilled port?

blocks.note: arch- as an adjective means chief or principal, as in arch-enemy
an angel is a private backer, especially of a theatre show

explanation.surface: A lead financier's hospitality includes serving the fortified wine cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the drink, but it is a harbour town: Archangel (Arkhangelsk) on the White Sea, icebound for much of the year.
explanation.definitionFit: Archangel is a northern Russian seaport whose harbour freezes in winter, hence a cold port.

clue.text: Ears blasted with CD that's divine

indicators.note: something blasted is blown apart, so its letters scatter into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone's ears are blasted by a disc they think is heavenly music.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacred and divine both describe something holy or belonging to God.

clue.text: Object after wild cat put out

indicators.note: wild suggests something out of control, so letters run riot into a different order
put out means disturbed or upset, another hint that letters are disordered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone goes after a feral cat that has been turned out of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Object' looks like a verb (to protest), but it is the noun. 'Wild cat' reads as one animal; 'wild' and 'put out' both signal the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: An artefact is a man-made object, especially one of historical interest.

clue.text: Advertising Standards Authority unimaginative really

blocks.note: ASA is the initialism of the UK advertising regulator
matter-of-fact means prosaic, unimaginative

explanation.surface: A complaint that the advertising watchdog is truly lacking in imagination.
explanation.walkthrough: The Advertising Standards Authority is Britain's watchdog for advertisements.
explanation.definitionFit: 'As a matter of fact' is an idiom meaning actually or in truth, used just like really.

clue.text: Voice disapproval with one in examination class

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the following word

blocks.note: to tut is to click the tongue in disapproval
an oral is a spoken examination
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A teacher tuts at a pupil sitting the test in class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Voice disapproval' reads as a speech instruction; it is the short noise of disapproval made with the tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: A tutorial is a small teaching session, a type of class with a tutor.

clue.text: Glare last from Chief Whip

indicators.note: last from asks for only the final letter of the next word

blocks.note: the final letter of chief
a lash is a whip

explanation.surface: The party's Chief Whip shoots one final hard stare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chief Whip' reads as the parliamentary office, but the two words are split. The Chief Whip enforces party discipline in the UK Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: A flash is a sudden burst of bright light, a dazzling glare.

clue.text: Writer to attend female relatives did you say?

indicators.note: asking what you said points to how the words are pronounced, not spelt

blocks.note: to serve is to attend; aunts are female relatives

explanation.surface: Someone checks whether they heard right about waiting on their aunts.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud in English, 'serve aunts' matches the Spanish surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Miguel de Cervantes was the Spanish novelist who wrote Don Quixote.

clue.text: Charming Charlie taken in with guile

indicators.note: taken in means absorbed, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet
craft is cunning, guile

explanation.surface: A charming man called Charlie was fooled by someone's cunning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charming' looks like an adjective describing Charlie; it is the definition, in its sense of casting spells. C sits inside WITH.
explanation.definitionFit: Charming in its old sense means casting spells, which is the practice of witchcraft.

clue.text: Excellent on river in Yorkshire

blocks.note: A1 means first-rate, written AI in crosswords
re means on or concerning

explanation.surface: Praise for something splendid on a Yorkshire river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aire is a river that flows through Leeds in Yorkshire, northern England.

clue.text: Weird American avoiding press and public

indicators.note: weird means strange or odd, so the letters come out in an odd order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An eccentric American celebrity shuns the media and the crowds.
explanation.definitionFit: In camera is a legal Latin phrase for proceedings held in private, closed to reporters and spectators.

clue.text: He runs back to devour warm food again

indicators.note: going back means the preceding words are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
to devour is to eat

explanation.surface: A man dashes home to wolf down his dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: To reheat is to make cooked food hot once more.

clue.text: Russian fighter touring north — in 7 21 he was 16!

indicators.note: touring means going around, so one word wraps the other

blocks.note: the MiG is a Russian fighter jet
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A Soviet jet circles northwards on a mission from an old adventure serial.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-references read Flash Gordon (7 and 21) and Merciless (16): Ming the Merciless is the villain.
explanation.definitionFit: Ming the Merciless is the tyrant of the planet Mongo in the Flash Gordon comics and films.

clue.text: Beefy hearts in Manitoba pickled

indicators.note: pickled means preserved but also drunk, so the letters stagger into disorder

blocks.note: H is the card-suit abbreviation for hearts
taken as written

explanation.surface: Bold hearts preserved in vinegar in a Canadian province.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beefy' looks like an adjective, but it is the nickname of a famous English cricketer.
explanation.definitionFit: Beefy was the nickname of Ian Botham, the England all-rounder cricketer.

clue.text: Mince meat twice for colleague

indicators.note: to mince is to chop finely, so the letters are cut up and rearranged

blocks.note: the word meat, written two times

explanation.surface: A cooking instruction to grind the meat a second time.
explanation.definitionFit: A teammate is a fellow member of a team, a colleague or co-worker.

clue.text: Is an ungrateful Frenchman so unfeeling?

blocks.note: merci is a Frenchman's word of thanks
the ungrateful one is without, or less, his thanks

explanation.surface: A question about whether a thankless Frenchman is cold-hearted.
explanation.walkthrough: A Frenchman who gives no thanks is 'merci-less', a pun on a word for unfeeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Merciless means showing no pity, which is cruelly unfeeling.

clue.text: Single sister with love interest in Bury

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
a nun is a religious sister
a date is someone you are romantically seeing

explanation.surface: An unattached nun has a boyfriend in the Lancashire town of Bury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bury' looks like the town near Manchester, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To inundate is to flood or overwhelm, so as to bury under a mass of something.

clue.text: Short crack in a certain ship?

blocks.note: first meaning: a brief joke or wisecrack
second meaning: read as ..., a single passenger ship

explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' suggests a split in a hull, but it means a quip; the question mark flags the split reading of the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-liner is a short witty remark, while a liner is a passenger ship, and one is a certain number.

clue.text: Quintessentially English girl made progress

blocks.note: first meaning: an English ..., the idealised fair-skinned English young woman
second meaning: went up, advanced

explanation.surface: A typical English girl got on in the world.
explanation.definitionFit: An English rose is the stereotype of a fresh English girl; rose is also the past tense of rise, to advance.

clue.text: Keep desiring person of easy virtue?

blocks.note: to want is to desire
on as in keep on, continuing

explanation.surface: Someone goes on lusting after a loose woman.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'want on' is to keep wanting, as in go on or carry on.
explanation.definitionFit: A wanton, as a dated noun, is a sexually promiscuous person.

clue.text: Henchman crossing road — is it Ramsay?

indicators.note: crossing here means spanning, with one word stretched around the other

blocks.note: a goon is a thug or henchman
Rd is the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: A heavy crosses the street: could it be the celebrity chef?
explanation.walkthrough: Gordon Ramsay is the famously foul-mouthed British TV chef; the question mark marks a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Gordon is the first name of Ramsay, so the forename is defined by one famous bearer.

clue.text: Maradona's two passes?

blocks.note: surface reading: a pair of passes of the ball by the Argentine footballer
setter's reading: two words that each mean pass, one as in pass away, one as in a turn in a game, together making the footballer's first name

explanation.walkthrough: Pass means die (pass away) and also go (have a turn), and together those spell the footballer's forename.
explanation.definitionFit: Diego Maradona was the Argentine football star, so his first name is what the clue asks for.

clue.text: Ruddy duck that's a wader?

blocks.note: ruddy and flaming are both mild British swearwords, euphemisms for bloody
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Asks whether the ruddy duck, a real species, counts as a wading bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy duck' is a real bird, which hides the split. Ruddy and flaming are British mild curses.
explanation.definitionFit: The flamingo is a long-legged pink bird that feeds by wading in shallow water.

clue.text: Lizard good on City floor?

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
EC is the postcode area of the City of London
to floor is to knock out, KO

explanation.surface: A lizard settles nicely on an office floor in the financial district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City floor' suggests a trading floor; the City is London's financial district, postcode EC.
explanation.definitionFit: A gecko is a small climbing lizard of warm countries.

clue.text: Spades with another tool — last product?

blocks.note: S is the card-suit abbreviation for spades
a hoe is a garden tool, another besides a spade

explanation.surface: A gardener's spade and hoe, perhaps the final item made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' looks like final, but a last is a cobbler's foot-shaped mould.
explanation.definitionFit: A cobbler shapes a shoe around a last, so the shoe is what the last produces.

clue.text: Mad Hatter cast with some difficulty

indicators.note: mad means crazy, so the letters are put in a crazy order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Casting the Mad Hatter role in a play proves hard work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad Hatter' reads as the Alice in Wonderland character, but 'Mad' is the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: At a stretch is an idiom meaning only with effort or by making allowances.

clue.text: Helpless monkey returned to hospital department

indicators.note: returned means sent back, so the short word is read backwards

blocks.note: a monkey can mean a mischievous child, an imp
taken as written
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: A distressed monkey is brought back to the hospital ward.
explanation.definitionFit: Impotent means powerless, unable to act, which is helpless.

clue.text: Wise man in wine store

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A sage found in an off-licence.
explanation.definitionFit: Nestor was the aged, wise counsellor of the Greeks in Homer's Iliad, so the name means a wise elder.
